source.title: Anchor function: a type of benchmark functions for studying language models
source.authors: Zhongwang Zhang; Zhiwei Wang; Jun-Jie Yao; Zhang-Chen Zhou; Xiaolong Li; E. Weinan; Zhi-Qin John Xu

record.tranche_reason: The paper mentions induction heads in its background and discussion, but does not measure or test induction behavior, in-context learning, or the timing of their emergence. Its own attention-mechanism findings concern shifting and broadcasting in anchor-function tasks.
record.gate_note: Induction heads and their proposed relation to in-context learning are described from cited work, not reported as this study's results. The paper's own attention-map findings on shifting and broadcasting are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not test the induction behavior or ICL claims.
record.test_reason: Induction heads appear only in related work and one remark in Section 5.6, citing Elhage et al. and Olsson et al. The paper's own mechanism results are first-layer shift and later-layer broadcast heads in a single-occurrence anchor task. That task is not repeated-token copying, so it tests no version. The reading-comprehension task (a1,x1,...,a → xk) is induction-like, but only accuracy is reported, with no head or mechanism analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors propose anchor functions as cheap, controlled benchmarks for studying language models. On identity learning, they find attention performs shift and broadcast operations, which they also report as common in Llama2. They add that the frequency principle and condensation help explain training behaviour.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates anchor functions and shift/broadcast attention operations; it does not reproduce or test the induction-head method or claims.
record.method_sensitivity: The attention-map shift changes with the anchor/key-item positional relation in the two-anchor identity task.

fits_no_version.finding: In the two-layer identity-learning task, first-layer heads shift tokens by the anchor–key offset (1 or 2 positions, set by the data structure). Second-layer heads broadcast the key-item information to the output position.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In anchor-function tasks, attention learns position-offset shift heads matched to the data structure, plus broadcast heads.

fits_no_version.finding: On one name-query prompt in Llama2, shallow heads show shift patterns and deep heads show broadcast patterns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large language models show shift heads in shallow layers and broadcast heads in deep layers.

fits_no_version.finding: All second-layer heads of a 4-layer, 12-head model have highly similar broadcast attention maps, which the authors attribute to condensation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Heads in the same layer converge to similar attention patterns (condensation).

record.problems: The study does not test induction heads or ICL. Its Llama2-6B example uses one stated prompt, and the layer number for the broadcast head is inconsistent between prose and figure caption.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported attention-map results were left out. General anchor-task accuracy, training curves, and other task results do not measure induction heads or ICL.

untested.parts: No previous-token/induction composition or [A][B]…[A]→[B] mechanism analysed. The shift head resembles a previous-token head, but the second layer broadcasts from an anchor position rather than matching a repeated token.
No training-time tracking of head formation, ICL or a loss bump.
No measurement of ICL by token index or its attribution to induction heads.
No search for induction heads across models. Llama2 maps are examined only for shift and broadcast patterns.
Data structure changes the shift offset (Section 5.2), but induction-head formation and ICL persistence are not measured.
No comparison of induction heads with other mechanisms for few-shot learning.

record.verdict_notes: Layer numbering for the Llama2 heads is inconsistent between captions and prose for both r7 and r8. The Llama2 evidence is qualitative and based on a single prompt. No version verdicts are given because the study does not test induction heads.

versions.untested_parts: No test of induction-head formation, composition with a previous-token head, or [A][B] … [A] → [B] behavior.
No training-time measurement of induction heads, ICL gain, or a corresponding loss-curve bump.
No test of induction heads as the mechanism behind most ICL in large transformers.
No survey or comparison of induction behavior across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
The study varies data and training setups for anchor tasks, not induction-head formation or persistence of ICL.
No test comparing induction heads with other mechanisms for few-shot task learning.
No analysis of whether induction-head formation consists of multiple transitions.

relation.reason: Related work describes induction heads and their proposed connection to in-context learning; Section 5.6 distinguishes induction from the operations studied here.

tranche.reason: The original experiments measure shift and broadcast operations in anchor tasks, not induction behavior or any listed claim version.
